records.greek: Ὁ οὖν Ἰησοῦς πρὸ ἓξ ἡμερῶν τοῦ πάσχα ἦλθεν εἰς Βηθανίαν, ὅπου ἦν Λάζαρος, ὃν ἤγειρεν ἐκ νεκρῶν Ἰησοῦς.
records.gloss: The therefore Jesus before six days of the Passover came to Bethany, where was Lazarus, whom raised out of dead [ones] Jesus.

L.1: So Jesus, six days before the Passover, came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus raised from [the] dead.

R.1: Six days before the Passover festival, Jesus came to Bethany. Lazarus was there, the man Jesus had raised from the dead.

decisions.choice: where Lazarus was, whom Jesus raised (SBLGNT)
alternatives: where Lazarus was, the one who had died, whom Jesus raised
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts, among them most later ones, add "the one who had died" after Lazarus's name. Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, with other early witnesses, do not have the words. They add nothing new, since the next clause says Jesus raised him from the dead, and look like a copyist's explanation. A footnote gives the longer reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: six days before the Passover: the start of the last week before Jesus's death
decisions.reason: This is the Passover that was near in 11:55, the third John names (2:13; 6:4). Jesus dies at this festival, on the day of Preparation (19:14, 31). From here John counts down to it: the next day comes in 12:12, and 13:1 opens with "before the feast of the Passover". Bethany was about two miles from Jerusalem (11:18), close enough for pilgrims to stay there.

decisions.choice: So: the story picks up after the leaders' orders of 11:57
alternatives: a strong "therefore" giving the reason for his coming
decisions.reason: The little word links this scene loosely to what went before. The chief priests and Pharisees had ordered anyone who knew where Jesus was to report it (11:57), and he had withdrawn to Ephraim (11:54). Now, with the festival near, he comes back to a village close to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: whom Jesus raised: John names Jesus again at the end of the sentence
decisions.reason: The sentence already began with Jesus as its subject, yet John repeats the name at the end, so that the man Lazarus is tied firmly to the one who raised him. That raising is what brings the crowds in verse 9 and the plot in verse 10.

decisions.choice: the man Jesus had raised (B, R); Lazarus was there (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the repeated name (meaning decision m4) and use "had raised", since the raising came before this visit. Readable makes two sentences and adds "festival" to Passover so a young reader knows what it was.

records.heading: Mary anoints Jesus

records.greek: ἐποίησαν οὖν αὐτῷ δεῖπνον ἐκεῖ, καὶ ἡ Μάρθα διηκόνει, ὁ δὲ Λάζαρος εἷς ἦν ἐκ τῶν ἀνακειμένων σὺν αὐτῷ·
records.gloss: Made therefore for him a dinner there, and the Martha was serving, the but Lazarus one was of the [ones] reclining with him;

L.2: So they made Him a dinner there, and Martha was serving, and Lazarus was one of those reclining [at table] with Him.

R.2: There they held a dinner for Jesus. Martha served the food, and Lazarus was one of the guests eating with Him.

decisions.choice: they: the people of the house, not named
alternatives: the village of Bethany as a whole
decisions.reason: John does not say who gave the dinner or whose house it was. Martha serves and her sister and brother are present, which suggests the family took part. Mark and Matthew place a dinner at Bethany two days before the Passover in the house of Simon the leper (Mark 14:1-3; Matthew 26:2-6), and many see the same event there. John's account does not depend on settling this.

decisions.choice: was serving: waiting on the guests at table
alternatives: serving in a wider sense, as a disciple
decisions.reason: The verb is the ordinary word for serving food and waiting on guests. The tense pictures her busy through the meal, as in the other story about the two sisters (Luke 10:40). Jesus later uses the same word for anyone who serves him (12:26).

decisions.choice: reclining: lying on couches around a low table, as guests did at a formal meal
alternatives: sitting on chairs at a table
decisions.reason: At a festive meal guests lay on their left side on couches or cushions, leaning on the elbow, with their feet stretched out away from the table. This is why Mary can reach Jesus's feet in verse 3, and why the disciple whom Jesus loved can lean back against him at the last supper (13:23-25).

decisions.choice: Lazarus at table: the man raised from death eating with the one who raised him
decisions.reason: John notes that Lazarus was among the guests. The man who was four days in the tomb (11:39) now shares an ordinary meal, which shows that he is truly alive. It also explains the crowds who come to see him (verse 9).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "my" and "me" when Jesus speaks of himself (verses 7-8). At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: gave a dinner, reclined at table (B); held a dinner, eating with (R)
decisions.reason: "Made a dinner" is the Greek idiom; "gave" or "held" is the natural way to say it. Balanced keeps the posture of the guests, which verse 3 needs (meaning decision m3); Readable simply says they were eating together.

records.greek: ἡ οὖν Μαριὰμ λαβοῦσα λίτραν μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς πολυτίμου ἤλειψεν τοὺς πόδας τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ ἐξέμαξεν ταῖς θριξὶν αὐτῆς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ· ἡ δὲ οἰκία ἐπληρώθη ἐκ τῆς ὀσμῆς τοῦ μύρου.
records.gloss: The therefore Mary having taken a pound of perfume of nard pure very costly anointed the feet of the Jesus and wiped off with the hairs of her the feet of him; the and house was filled from the fragrance of the perfume.

L.3: So Mary, having taken a pound of perfumed oil of pure nard, very costly, anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped His feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfumed oil.

R.3: Then Mary took about 12 ounces of perfume made from pure nard, a sweet-smelling oil that cost a great deal. She poured it on Jesus's feet and wiped them with her hair. The sweet smell of the perfume filled the whole house.

decisions.choice: a pound: a Roman pound, about 327 grams (about 11.5 ounces)
decisions.reason: The word is the Roman pound, lighter than the modern pound of 16 ounces. It is a large amount of perfume, far more than a person would use at one time, and it was worth about a year's wages (verse 5). John uses the same measure for the hundred pounds of spices Nicodemus brings for Jesus's burial (19:39).

decisions.choice: pure: genuine, unmixed nard
alternatives: a place or plant name, perhaps from the pistachio
decisions.reason: The adjective is found almost only here and in the same phrase in Mark 14:3, so its meaning is not certain. It most likely comes from the root for "faith" and "trust", giving "genuine" or "pure", nard that had not been mixed with cheaper oils. Some take it from the name of the pistachio tree or of a place, and others as "liquid". The sense "genuine" fits the stress on the oil's great cost. A footnote gives the other views.

decisions.choice: perfumed oil of nard: a costly fragrant oil from the nard plant
decisions.reason: The first word is perfumed oil, as in 11:2, which already refers to this anointing. Nard (spikenard) was an aromatic oil made from the root of a plant that grows in the Himalayas, imported from far away and very expensive. It is named in the Song of Songs as a precious perfume (Song of Songs 1:12; 4:13-14).

decisions.choice: anointing the feet and wiping them with her hair: an act of humble, lavish devotion
alternatives: the usual courtesy of a host to a guest
decisions.reason: A host might give a guest water for the feet or put a little oil on the head (Luke 7:44-46). Mary pours costly perfume on Jesus's feet and wipes them with her own hair. Caring for feet was the work of a slave, and a respectable woman did not usually let down her hair in company, so the act shows both humility and great love. Mark and Matthew say the woman poured the perfume on Jesus's head (Mark 14:3; Matthew 26:7); John tells of the feet. With so much perfume, both may have happened, but each writer tells what matters for his account. In John the scene looks ahead to Jesus washing his disciples' feet (13:4-5).

decisions.choice: {{units:about 12 ounces|a Roman pound}}
decisions.reason: A modern reader takes "a pound" as 16 ounces, so Balanced and Readable give the weight in ounces by default (meaning decision m1), and the units setting shows "a Roman pound". Literal keeps the ancient unit.

decisions.choice: perfumed oil, anointed (L, B); perfume, poured it on (R)
decisions.reason: The same words as in 11:2, which refers ahead to this anointing, so the two verses match at every level. Readable says plainly what anointing was here, as 11:2 does, and explains nard briefly.

records.greek: λέγει δὲ Ἰούδας ὁ Ἰσκαριώτης εἷς τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ, ὁ μέλλων αὐτὸν παραδιδόναι·
records.gloss: Says but Judas the Iscariot, one of the disciples of him, the [one] being about him to hand over;

L.4: But Judas Iscariot, one of His disciples, the one who was about to hand Him over, says,

R.4: But one of Jesus's disciples, Judas Iscariot, spoke up. He was the one who would soon betray Jesus. He said,

decisions.choice: hand over: betray him to his enemies
alternatives: hand over, with no thought of betrayal
decisions.reason: As in 6:64 and 6:71, the verb means to hand someone over. Used of Judas, one of Jesus's own disciples, it means betrayal (13:2, 21; 18:2-5).

decisions.choice: the one who was about to: what Judas would soon do
alternatives: the one who intended to, at this moment
decisions.reason: The participle looks ahead from the narrator's point of view, as in 6:71. It names Judas by the deed for which he is remembered; it does not say he had already decided on it at this dinner.

decisions.choice: Judas Iscariot (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts name Judas here as "son of Simon", as he is named in 6:71 and 13:2, 26. The shorter name is in Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus and early papyri. A footnote gives the longer reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: one of his disciples: one of Jesus's own followers
decisions.reason: John stresses that the objection comes from inside the circle of disciples, as he did when he first named Judas (6:70-71). Mark and Matthew say some of those present, or the disciples, were angry (Mark 14:4; Matthew 26:8); John names the one who spoke.

decisions.choice: spoke up (B); spoke up ... He said (R)
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("he says") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This is the only such verb in the passage.

decisions.choice: hand over (L); betray (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 6:64 and 6:71 (meaning decision m1). Literal keeps the plain sense of the verb; Balanced and Readable say what Judas's handing over was. Readable names Jesus to make clear who would be betrayed.

records.greek: Διὰ τί τοῦτο τὸ μύρον οὐκ ἐπράθη τριακοσίων δηναρίων καὶ ἐδόθη πτωχοῖς;
records.gloss: Why this the perfume not was sold of three hundred denarii and was given to poor [ones]?

L.5: "Why was this perfumed oil not sold for three hundred denarii and given to [the] poor?"

R.5: "This perfume could have been sold for about a year's pay. Why was it not sold, and the money given to poor people?"

decisions.choice: three hundred denarii: about a year's wages
decisions.reason: A denarius was a silver coin, the usual pay for a laborer's day of work (Matthew 20:2). Three hundred denarii was the pay for about a year of working days, once Sabbaths and festivals are left out. Philip reckoned that two hundred denarii would not buy enough bread for the crowd (6:7); this perfume was worth more. Mark has "more than three hundred denarii" (Mark 14:5).

decisions.choice: given to the poor: gifts to the poor, especially at Passover
decisions.reason: Giving to the poor was a duty of the law (Deuteronomy 15:7-11) and a custom of the Passover season. At the last supper some disciples thought Judas had gone out to give something to the poor (13:29).

decisions.choice: Why ... not: a question that is really a complaint
alternatives: a real request for an explanation
decisions.reason: The question blames Mary for wasting the perfume. Jesus answers it as a rebuke when he says "Leave her" (verse 7), and the narrator gives Judas's true motive in verse 6.

decisions.choice: {{units:about a year's wages|three hundred denarii}} (B); {{units:about a year's pay|three hundred denarii}} (R)
decisions.reason: As in 6:7: the coin means nothing to most readers, so Balanced and Readable give its value in wages by default, and the units setting shows "three hundred denarii". Literal always keeps the coin. The number stays in words, as in 6:7.

decisions.choice: the money given to the poor
decisions.reason: It was the money from the sale, not the oil, that would have gone to the poor; Balanced and Readable say so.

records.greek: εἶπεν δὲ τοῦτο οὐχ ὅτι περὶ τῶν πτωχῶν ἔμελεν αὐτῷ, ἀλλ’ ὅτι κλέπτης ἦν καὶ τὸ γλωσσόκομον ἔχων τὰ βαλλόμενα ἐβάσταζεν.
records.gloss: Said but this not that about the poor it was a care to him, but that a thief he was and the money box having the [things] being put in he was carrying off.

L.6: But he said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, he used to carry off what was put into it.

R.6: Judas did not say this because he cared about poor people. He said it because he was a thief. He was in charge of the group's money box, and he often stole the money people put in it.

decisions.choice: he said this, not because he cared: the narrator tells Judas's real motive
decisions.reason: John alone among the Gospels gives this comment. He writes looking back, knowing what Judas became, and shows that the concern for the poor was a cover.

decisions.choice: money box: the box in which the group's money was kept
decisions.reason: The word first meant a case for the mouthpieces of musical instruments and came to mean any box or case, especially one for money. Judas kept it for Jesus and the disciples (13:29). Gifts from supporters went into it, and money for food and for the poor came out of it.

decisions.choice: carry off: take away for himself, steal
alternatives: only carry, as the keeper of the box
decisions.reason: The verb means to carry or bear, and can also mean to carry off or take away, as in 20:15, where Mary thinks someone has carried Jesus's body away. Since John has just called Judas a thief, the second sense is meant here: he carried the box, and he carried off what was in it. The tense shows that he did it habitually.

decisions.choice: a thief: the same word Jesus used for the thief who comes to steal
decisions.reason: In 10:1, 8, 10 the thief is the one who comes only to steal and destroy, in contrast to the good shepherd. John uses the same word of Judas, the disciple who will hand the shepherd over.

decisions.choice: used to carry off (L); used to take for himself (B); often stole (R)
decisions.reason: Every level gives the sense of stealing (meaning decision m3). Literal keeps "carry" with "off", which still shows the verb's picture; Readable says plainly that he stole.

decisions.choice: was in charge of (B, R); the group's (R)
decisions.reason: "Having the money box" means he kept the group's money (13:29). Balanced and Readable say so; Readable adds whose money it was.

records.greek: εἶπεν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἄφες αὐτήν, ἵνα εἰς τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ ἐνταφιασμοῦ μου τηρήσῃ αὐτό·
records.gloss: Said therefore the Jesus, "Leave her, so that for the day of the burial-preparation of me she may keep it;

L.7: So Jesus said, "Let her be, in order that she may keep it for the day of My preparation for burial.

R.7: Jesus said, "Leave her alone. She was meant to keep this perfume for the day when My body is made ready to be buried.

decisions.choice: she was to keep it for the day of my burial: she did not sell it, and her anointing now is part of preparing his body for burial
alternatives: Let her keep the rest of it for the day of my burial
Let her alone, so that she may keep the memory of this for the day of my burial
decisions.reason: The Greek is brief and hard: "Leave her, so that for the day of my burial she may keep it." Since Mary has just used the perfume, "keep it" is puzzling. One reading takes the words as the purpose of her having kept it rather than selling it: it was kept for this, and by pouring it out now she prepares his body for burial ahead of time, as Mark says (Mark 14:8). A second reading supposes that only part was used, and Jesus tells them to let her keep the rest for his burial; but John says nothing of a remainder, and the women do not anoint his body in John (19:39-40). A third takes "it" as the memory of what she did. The first fits the context best, but the evidence is evenly balanced. A footnote gives the other readings.

decisions.choice: so that she may keep it (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "she has kept it for the day of my burial", without "so that", which is easier to understand. The harder wording is in early papyri, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and the easier one looks like a correction. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: burial: preparing a body for burial
decisions.reason: The noun means the laying out and preparing of a body for the tomb, with spices and wrappings. John uses the related verb of what Joseph and Nicodemus did for Jesus's body, "as is the custom of the Jews to prepare for burial" (19:40). Mary's act looks ahead to his death, now close (12:23-24).

decisions.choice: Leave her: let her alone, stop troubling her
decisions.reason: The command answers Judas's complaint: Jesus defends Mary and tells the objectors to stop finding fault with her, as in Mark 14:6.

decisions.choice: She was to keep it (B); She was meant to keep (R)
alternatives: so that she may keep it (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable follow meaning decision m1: the perfume was kept for this purpose. "Was to keep" keeps the sense of purpose without following the variant "she has kept it". Literal keeps the Greek purpose clause and its ambiguity.

decisions.choice: my preparation for burial (L); my body is prepared for burial (B); my body is made ready to be buried (R)
decisions.reason: The noun means the preparing of a body, not only the burial (meaning decision m3); every level says so.

records.greek: τοὺς πτωχοὺς γὰρ πάντοτε ἔχετε μεθ’ ἑαυτῶν, ἐμὲ δὲ οὐ πάντοτε ἔχετε.
records.gloss: The poor for always you have with yourselves, me but not always you have.

L.8: For the poor you have always with you, but Me you do not have always."

R.8: Poor people will always be with you. But I will not always be here with you."

decisions.choice: the poor you always have: an echo of Deuteronomy 15:11
decisions.reason: The law says that the poor will never cease from the land, and therefore commands Israel to open its hand to them (Deuteronomy 15:11). Jesus does not set aside that command; he says that there will always be time to help the poor.

decisions.choice: me you do not always have: Jesus will soon go away by his death
alternatives: a claim that he matters more than the poor
decisions.reason: The contrast is one of time. Jesus has said he will be with them only a little longer (7:33; 13:33). Mary's gift fits the short time that is left before his death (verse 7).

decisions.choice: the verse is part of the text (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Codex Bezae and the Sinaitic Syriac leave out the whole verse. Nearly all other manuscripts have it. Some think it was added from the same saying in Matthew 26:11 and Mark 14:7, but the evidence for it is strong. A footnote notes the omission. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: I will not always be with you
alternatives: me you do not always have (Literal)
you will not always have me
decisions.reason: "You do not always have me" means that Jesus will not be with them for long (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable say that directly and look to the future, which the present tense implies here. The pronoun "I" takes no setting.

records.greek: Ἔγνω οὖν ὄχλος πολὺς ἐκ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ὅτι ἐκεῖ ἐστιν, καὶ ἦλθον οὐ διὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν μόνον, ἀλλ’ ἵνα καὶ τὸν Λάζαρον ἴδωσιν ὃν ἤγειρεν ἐκ νεκρῶν.
records.gloss: Knew therefore crowd large of the Jews that there he is, and they came not because of the Jesus only, but so that also the Lazarus they might see whom he raised from dead [ones].

L.9: So a large crowd of the Jews learned that He was there, and they came, not on account of Jesus only, but so that they might also see Lazarus, whom He raised from [the] dead.

R.9: A big crowd of the Jews found out that Jesus was in Bethany, so they went there. They came to see Jesus, but they also wanted to see Lazarus, the man Jesus had raised from the dead.

decisions.choice: the Jews: Jewish people from Jerusalem and the area around it
decisions.reason: This crowd is not the authorities, who are named separately in verse 10 and plot against those who believe. They are people who, like the mourners of 11:19 and 11:45, came out from Jerusalem, two miles away (11:18), many of them pilgrims gathering for the Passover (11:55). Many of them came to believe (verse 11).

decisions.choice: a large crowd, without the article (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Some important manuscripts have the article, "the large crowd", in an unusual position. The meaning is much the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: that he was there: the words as the crowd heard them
decisions.reason: Greek keeps the tense of the words that were reported, so the Greek says "that he is there". It is not the historic present of storytelling.

decisions.choice: to see Lazarus also: they came to see the sign for themselves
decisions.reason: The raising of Lazarus had made him famous. People came to see the living man as well as Jesus, and this crowd spreads the news when Jesus enters Jerusalem (12:17-18).

decisions.choice: a large crowd of the Jews (B); a big crowd of the Jews (R)
decisions.reason: Here the word means the people of Jerusalem and the crowds there (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable keep the word John wrote and tie it to the crowd present, as 11:45 does; no footnote is needed.

decisions.choice: Jesus was there (B); Jesus was in Bethany (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus for clarity; Readable also names the village, from verse 1.

records.greek: ἐβουλεύσαντο δὲ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς ἵνα καὶ τὸν Λάζαρον ἀποκτείνωσιν, ὅτι πολλοὶ δι’ αὐτὸν ὑπῆγον τῶν Ἰουδαίων καὶ ἐπίστευον εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν.
records.gloss: Planned but the chief priests that also the Lazarus they might kill, \v 11 because many on account of him were going away of the Jews and were believing in the Jesus.

L.10: But the chief priests planned that they might kill Lazarus also,
L.11: because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.

R.10: So the leading priests made plans to kill Lazarus too.
R.11: They wanted him dead because many of the Jews were leaving them and believing in Jesus. Lazarus was the reason.

decisions.choice: were going away: leaving the authorities and their way, to follow Jesus
alternatives: going off to Bethany to see Jesus and Lazarus
decisions.reason: The verb means to go away or depart. It can simply describe people going out from Jerusalem to Bethany, as the crowd did (verse 9). But the authorities are alarmed, and the verb is joined to "believing", so it most likely means that people were leaving them and their leadership, as some disciples "went back" from Jesus in 6:66. The other sense remains possible. A footnote gives it.

decisions.choice: the Jews: Jewish people of Jerusalem, as in verse 9
decisions.reason: These are people who were turning to Jesus, set against the chief priests. The word means the people, not their leaders.

decisions.choice: the chief priests: the high priest and the leading priestly families; Lazarus also, as well as Jesus
decisions.reason: The council had already decided to kill Jesus (11:53). Now the chief priests plan to kill Lazarus too, since he is the living proof of the sign that is drawing people to Jesus. The leading priests were mostly Sadducees, who denied that the dead rise (Acts 23:8), though John does not give that as their reason.

decisions.choice: were going away and believing: something going on and spreading
decisions.reason: Both verbs are in the imperfect: people kept leaving and coming to believe in Jesus, one after another. The key term is believe "in" Jesus (3:16; 11:45).

decisions.choice: leaving them
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable follow meaning decision m1 and say whom the people were leaving: the authorities. Literal keeps the open "going away". This choice is uncertain; the footnote on m1 gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: leading priests
decisions.reason: As in 7:45 and 11:47, Readable says "leading priests", which a young reader can follow, and adds that Lazarus was the reason, which Balanced keeps as "on his account".

records.greek: Τῇ ἐπαύριον ὁ ὄχλος πολὺς ὁ ἐλθὼν εἰς τὴν ἑορτήν, ἀκούσαντες ὅτι ἔρχεται ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα, ἔλαβον τὰ βαΐα τῶν φοινίκων καὶ ἐξῆλθον εἰς ὑπάντησιν αὐτῷ, καὶ ἐκραύγαζον· Ὡσαννά, εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου, καὶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τοῦ Ἰσραήλ.
records.gloss: On the next day the crowd great the [one] having come to the feast, having heard that is coming the Jesus into Jerusalem, \v 13 took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meeting him, and were crying out, "Hosanna, blessed the [one] coming in name of Lord, and the king of the Israel."

L.12: On the next day the large crowd that had come to the feast, having heard that Jesus is coming into Jerusalem,
L.13: took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meet Him, and they were shouting, "Hosanna! Blessed [is] the [one] coming in [the] name of [the] Lord, and the King of Israel!"

R.12: The next day the large crowd that had come for the Passover festival heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem.
R.13: So they took branches from the palm trees and went out to meet Him. They kept shouting, "Hosanna! Praise God! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! He is the King of Israel!"

decisions.choice: Hosanna: a Hebrew cry, "save, please", which had become a shout of praise and welcome
alternatives: a plain plea for rescue, "save us"
decisions.reason: The word comes from Psalm 118:25, "Save us, we pray, O LORD". Psalm 118 belongs to the Hallel psalms (113-118), sung at the great festivals, Passover among them, so the cry was well known to pilgrims. By this time it was used to acclaim God and the one he sends, as here, where it stands with "Blessed is ..." rather than with a request. The old sense, a call on God to save, still lies behind it, and fits a crowd that hopes for its king.

decisions.choice: the crowd's words quote Psalm 118:25-26
decisions.reason: In the psalm the words welcome the one who comes up to the house of the LORD, and the priests answer with a blessing from the temple (Psalm 118:26). The crowd uses the festival's own psalm to welcome Jesus as he comes into the city. Matthew 21:9, Mark 11:9-10 and Luke 19:38 give the same cry.

decisions.choice: in the name of the Lord: sent by God and coming with his authority; in Psalm 118:26 "Lord" stands for God's own name, the LORD
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew of Psalm 118:26 the word is the divine name. To come in someone's name is to come as that person's representative. Jesus says he has come in his Father's name and does his works in it (5:43; 10:25), so the acclaim is truer than the crowd knows.

decisions.choice: "the King of Israel" is the crowd's addition to the psalm
decisions.reason: Psalm 118 does not have these words. Zephaniah 3:15 calls the LORD "the King of Israel" in the midst of Jerusalem, and the next verse tells Zion not to fear, words John's quotation echoes in verse 15. Nathanael gave Jesus the same title (1:49); after the feeding of the five thousand the crowd wanted to make him king by force (6:15), and the cross will carry the title "King of the Jews" (19:19).

decisions.choice: and: "that is", naming the one who comes
alternatives: and: a second person, besides the one who comes
decisions.reason: The one who comes and the King of Israel are the same person, Jesus. The joining word adds a title, not a second figure.

decisions.choice: palm branches: a sign of national rejoicing and victory
alternatives: ordinary green branches, with no special meaning
decisions.reason: Palms were carried in Jewish celebrations: when Simon entered the citadel of Jerusalem in triumph (1 Maccabees 13:51), and when the temple was cleansed and rededicated (2 Maccabees 10:7); palm branches were also used at the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40). Waving them before Jesus greets him as a victorious king. John alone says the branches were from palm trees.

decisions.choice: went out to meet him: the formal welcome given to an arriving ruler
decisions.reason: In the ancient world a city's people went out along the road to greet a king or other great visitor and escort him in. The crowd gives Jesus that kind of welcome.

decisions.choice: Hosanna (every level); Readable adds "Praise God!"
decisions.reason: "Hosanna" is the word the crowd shouted and is known from worship, so every level keeps it. Readable adds "Praise God!" to show how the shout was used (meaning decision m1). It does not translate the word's origin, "save, please", which a reader would take as a call for help.

decisions.choice: Lord
decisions.reason: As at 1:23: the style guide keeps "the LORD" for the divine name in the Old Testament itself. Here the Gospel quotes the psalm with the Greek word "Lord"; meaning decision m3 says whom it means. The reader's divine-name setting is not used in the New Testament.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} (to meet him); no setting on "the one who comes" or "the King of Israel"
decisions.reason: The pronoun refers to Jesus and takes the setting. "The one who comes" and "the King of Israel" also mean Jesus, as the narrator shows in verses 14-16, but they are a noun phrase and a title, not pronouns, so no setting applies. In Readable "He is the King of Israel" starts a sentence and is written plain.

decisions.choice: the Passover festival
decisions.reason: The festival is the Passover named in 11:55 and 12:1; Readable names it. Balanced says "festival" for the Greek word for a feast day, which English readers might take to mean a meal.

records.heading: The king comes to Jerusalem

records.greek: εὑρὼν δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὀνάριον ἐκάθισεν ἐπ’ αὐτό, καθώς ἐστιν γεγραμμένον·
records.gloss: Having found and the Jesus a little donkey sat on it, as is having been written:

L.14: And Jesus, having found a young donkey, sat on it, as it is written:

R.14: Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it. This was just what the Scriptures had said would happen:

decisions.choice: young donkey
decisions.reason: The word is a diminutive of the word for donkey. Diminutives of this kind often lost their force, but verse 15 calls the animal "a donkey's colt", so a young animal is meant.

decisions.choice: riding a donkey: royal, but not warlike
decisions.reason: Donkeys and mules were ridden by Israel's leaders and kings in peace: Solomon rode David's mule to be anointed king (1 Kings 1:33-38), and judges had sons riding donkeys (Judges 10:4; 12:14). A conqueror came on a war horse. By choosing a donkey, Jesus accepts the welcome as king, and shows what kind of king he is (meaning decision m3 on verse 15).

decisions.choice: Jesus found a donkey and sat on it after the crowd had come out to greet him
decisions.reason: John tells the story briefly and in a different order from the other Gospels, where the disciples fetch the animal before the crowd's acclaim (Mark 11:1-10; Matthew 21:1-9; Luke 19:29-38). Here the crowd hails him first, and then Jesus mounts the donkey. His action may be meant as an answer to their welcome: he is their king, but not a king of war. The order is clear; how much John means by it is less certain.

decisions.choice: just as Scripture says (B); This was just what the Scriptures had said would happen (R)
decisions.reason: The phrase introduces a quotation from Scripture, and the tense means that the words stand written and still hold. Balanced and Readable name Scripture, since "it is written" alone may not tell a modern reader that a Bible quotation follows. Literal keeps the Greek form.

records.greek: Μὴ φοβοῦ, θυγάτηρ Σιών· ἰδοὺ ὁ βασιλεύς σου ἔρχεται, καθήμενος ἐπὶ πῶλον ὄνου.
records.gloss: Not be afraid, daughter of Zion; behold, the king of you is coming, sitting on a colt of a donkey.

L.15: "Do not be afraid, daughter of Zion; look, your king is coming, sitting on a colt of a donkey."

R.15: "People of Jerusalem, do not be afraid! Look! Your king is coming, riding on a young donkey!"

decisions.choice: the quotation is from Zechariah 9:9, shortened
decisions.reason: Zechariah 9:9 reads, "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Look, your king comes to you, righteous and bringing salvation, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey." John keeps the king and the donkey and leaves out the rest. Matthew 21:5 quotes the same verse.

decisions.choice: "Do not be afraid" in place of Zechariah's "Rejoice greatly": most likely from Zephaniah 3:16
alternatives: Isaiah 40:9 ("do not fear ... Here is your God")
John's own wording, with no second passage in mind
decisions.reason: Zephaniah 3:14-16 tells the daughter of Zion to rejoice because "the King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst", and says to Jerusalem, "Do not fear, Zion." The crowd has just used the title King of Israel (verse 13), which makes Zephaniah a likely source. Isaiah 40:9 also tells Zion not to fear and announces God's coming. John does not say which passage he has in mind.

decisions.choice: daughter of Zion: Jerusalem and its people
alternatives: a young woman of the city
decisions.reason: The prophets speak of Jerusalem as a woman, "daughter Zion" (Isaiah 1:8; Zechariah 9:9). Zion is the hill of the city and the temple, and the phrase stands for the whole city and the people who live there.

decisions.choice: a king who comes in peace, not on a war horse
decisions.reason: The next verse of Zechariah says that God will cut off the chariot and the war horse from Jerusalem, and that the king will speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). The donkey is part of that picture. The king John's readers see is the one who will be lifted up on the cross (12:32-33) and whose kingdom is not from this world (18:36).

decisions.choice: a donkey's colt: one young donkey
alternatives: two animals, a donkey and its colt
decisions.reason: Zechariah's Hebrew names the animal twice in parallel lines, "on a donkey, on a colt". Matthew 21:2-7 tells of two animals; John speaks of one, the young donkey of verse 14.

decisions.choice: People of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom (meaning decision m3), since a young reader would take "daughter" as one girl. Literal and Balanced keep the prophet's phrase.

decisions.choice: Look
decisions.reason: The word calls for attention. The style guide does not use "behold". There is no setting on "your" or "your king": "your" refers to the city, and "king" is a noun, not a pronoun for Jesus.

records.greek: ταῦτα οὐκ ἔγνωσαν αὐτοῦ οἱ μαθηταὶ τὸ πρῶτον, ἀλλ’ ὅτε ἐδοξάσθη Ἰησοῦς τότε ἐμνήσθησαν ὅτι ταῦτα ἦν ἐπ’ αὐτῷ γεγραμμένα καὶ ταῦτα ἐποίησαν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: These things not understood of him the disciples at the first, but when was glorified Jesus, then they remembered that these things were about him having been written and these things they did to him.

L.16: These things His disciples did not understand at the first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about Him and [that] they had done these things to Him.

R.16: At first His disciples did not understand what all this meant. But later Jesus was glorified through His death and resurrection. Then they remembered that Scripture had said these things about Him, and that they had done these very things for Him.

decisions.choice: did not understand: did not grasp what the events meant
alternatives: did not know: were unaware of what happened
decisions.reason: The disciples saw all of it. What they did not see at the time was that the welcome and the donkey fulfilled Scripture and showed who Jesus was.

decisions.choice: was glorified: Jesus's death, resurrection and return to the Father, seen as one event
decisions.reason: In John, Jesus is glorified in his "hour": the Son of Man is glorified when, like a grain of wheat, he dies and bears fruit (12:23-24; 13:31-32), and he returns to the glory he had with the Father (17:1, 5). The Spirit was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified (7:39). The passive points to God as the one who glorifies him (17:1).

decisions.choice: the disciples understood only after Jesus was glorified
decisions.reason: John says the same in 2:22, after the resurrection, and Jesus promises that the Spirit will remind the disciples of all he said (14:26). The light of Easter showed them that Scripture had spoken of these things.

decisions.choice: they had done these things to him: "they" left general, the people who welcomed him, the disciples perhaps among them
decisions.reason: The nearest subject is the disciples, who remembered. But in John it is the crowd that went out with palm branches and shouted, and Jesus himself found the donkey. John may use "they" loosely for those who took part, as the other Gospels have the disciples fetching the animal and joining the shout (Luke 19:35-37). Every level keeps "they".

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: Each pronoun refers to Jesus and takes the setting.

decisions.choice: for him
decisions.reason: What was done was an honor: the welcome, the branches and the acclaim. In English "done to him" can sound like harm, so Balanced and Readable say "for him". Literal keeps "to him".

decisions.choice: glorified through {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death and resurrection
decisions.reason: Readable says what "glorified" refers to here (meaning decision m2), since a young reader would not know. The return to the Father belongs to the same glory (17:5); the death and resurrection are named because they are what made the disciples remember (2:22).

records.greek: ἐμαρτύρει οὖν ὁ ὄχλος ὁ ὢν μετ’ αὐτοῦ ὅτε τὸν Λάζαρον ἐφώνησεν ἐκ τοῦ μνημείου καὶ ἤγειρεν αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν.
records.gloss: Was testifying therefore the crowd the [one] being with him when the Lazarus he called out of the tomb and raised him out of dead [ones].

L.17: So the crowd that was with Him when He called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him out of [the] dead was testifying.

R.17: The people who had been with Jesus when He called Lazarus out of the tomb and brought him back to life kept telling others what they had seen.

decisions.choice: when (hote; SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Vaticanus, read "when": the crowd who were with him when he called Lazarus kept testifying. Some, including an early papyrus and Codex Bezae, read "that": the crowd who were with him kept testifying that he had called Lazarus from the tomb. The two words differ by one letter, and the sense is close. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: kept testifying: the imperfect tense, an ongoing witness
decisions.reason: The tense shows continuing action: they went on telling what they had seen. Testifying is a key theme in John: John the Baptist, the works of Jesus, the Scriptures and the Father all testify to him (1:7; 5:31-39). These eyewitnesses are added to them.

decisions.choice: this crowd: the people who had been at Bethany, not the festival crowd of verse 12
alternatives: the same crowd as in verses 12 and 18
decisions.reason: John describes this crowd as the people who were with Jesus at the tomb (11:42, 45). The crowd in verse 18 is the one that "had heard" of the sign, the pilgrims of verse 12. The first group's testimony is why the second went out to meet him.

decisions.choice: raised: Jesus raised Lazarus (active)
decisions.reason: The verb is active, with Jesus as subject, as in 12:1, 9: he is the resurrection and the life (11:25). Contrast 2:22, where Jesus himself "was raised".

decisions.choice: testifying to what they had seen (B); kept telling others what they had seen (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek verb has no object; Balanced and Readable say what the crowd testified to, the raising of Lazarus they had seen. Readable uses plain words for "testify". Literal keeps the verb alone.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: The pronouns that refer to Jesus take the setting; "him" for Lazarus does not. Readable writes "with Jesus" so that the two men are not confused, and "brought him back to life" for "raised him from the dead".

records.greek: διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὑπήντησεν αὐτῷ ὁ ὄχλος ὅτι ἤκουσαν τοῦτο αὐτὸν πεποιηκέναι τὸ σημεῖον.
records.gloss: Because of this also met him the crowd, because they heard this him to have done the sign.

L.18: Because of this also the crowd met Him, because they heard [that] He had done this sign.

R.18: This is also why the crowd came out to meet Him. They had heard that He had done this sign, raising Lazarus from death.

decisions.choice: because of this ... because: the reason is given by the clause that follows
alternatives: "this" pointing back to the testimony of verse 17
decisions.reason: "This" points forward to "because they heard": hearing of the sign is why they came. "Also" adds this reason to what verse 17 has said, and the two verses together show the testimony spreading from one crowd to the other.

decisions.choice: the crowd: the festival crowd of verse 12; "they" heard
decisions.reason: The crowd is singular but "they heard" is plural: John thinks of the many people in it. These are the pilgrims who went out with palm branches (verses 12-13), and their reason is now given.

decisions.choice: this sign: the raising of Lazarus
decisions.reason: The raising of Lazarus is the last and greatest sign in John before Jesus's hour. It shows him as the resurrection and the life (11:25-26). It also led the council to plan his death (11:47-53), so the sign that brings the crowd out to meet him is the sign that leads to the cross.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Each pronoun refers to Jesus and takes the setting. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain.

decisions.choice: raising Lazarus from death
decisions.reason: Readable names the sign (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: οἱ οὖν Φαρισαῖοι εἶπαν πρὸς ἑαυτούς· Θεωρεῖτε ὅτι οὐκ ὠφελεῖτε οὐδέν· ἴδε ὁ κόσμος ὀπίσω αὐτοῦ ἀπῆλθεν.
records.gloss: The therefore Pharisees said to themselves, "You see that not you are gaining nothing; look, the world after him went away."

L.19: So the Pharisees said to one another, "You see that you are gaining nothing at all; look, the world has gone off after Him."

R.19: So the Pharisees said to each other, "You can see that nothing you do is working. Look, the whole world is following Him!"

decisions.choice: the world: everyone, a complaint that exaggerates
decisions.reason: The Pharisees mean that the crowds have gone over to Jesus. John lets the words say more than they intend: the world is what God loves and what Jesus came to save (3:16-17; 4:42), and in the next verse some Greeks come asking to see him (12:20-21). The council had feared the same thing, that "everyone will believe in him" (11:48), and Caiaphas, too, said more than he knew (11:49-52).

decisions.choice: you are gaining nothing: your efforts are getting you nowhere
alternatives: you are no help at all
decisions.reason: The verb means to help, benefit or gain, and the Greek doubles the negative for emphasis. The council had decided to kill Jesus and had ordered that anyone who knew where he was should report it (11:53, 57), and still the crowds went out to welcome him.

decisions.choice: You see: a statement
decisions.reason: The Greek form can be read either way, and the sense is much the same: they point to what is plain before them. The statement fits a complaint to one another.

decisions.choice: gone after him: become his followers
decisions.reason: To go after someone is to follow him as a disciple or supporter (compare 1:37; Mark 1:20). The past tense speaks as though it had already happened, which adds to the alarm of the words.

decisions.choice: the whole world
decisions.reason: "The world" is kept (key term), with "whole" added so that the line reads in English as the exaggerated complaint it is (meaning decision m1). Literal keeps "the world" alone.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: The pronoun refers to Jesus and takes the setting, as elsewhere in the narrative, though the speakers are his opponents.

records.greek: Ἦσαν δὲ Ἕλληνές τινες ἐκ τῶν ἀναβαινόντων ἵνα προσκυνήσωσιν ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ·
records.gloss: There were now Greeks certain among the [ones] going up that they might worship at the feast;

L.20: Now there were certain Greeks among those going up so that they might worship at the feast;

R.20: Some Greeks were among the people who had come up to Jerusalem to worship at the Passover festival.

decisions.choice: Greeks: non-Jews, people of the Greek-speaking world
decisions.reason: The word is used of Gentiles in general, as in 7:35, where the speakers set "the Greeks" beside the Jews scattered among them. Greek-speaking Jews were called by a different word (Acts 6:1). These visitors are Gentiles, which is why their coming matters: Jesus answers it by speaking of his hour and of drawing all people to himself (12:23, 32).

decisions.choice: Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God and came up to Jerusalem for the feast
decisions.reason: Those "going up" are the pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem for the festival, the Passover of 11:55 and 12:1. Gentiles who honored the God of Israel without becoming Jews (Acts 10:2; 17:4) could worship in the outer court of the temple but not go further in. Whether these Greeks were such worshipers or full converts the text does not say; that they came to worship shows that they honored Israel's God.

decisions.choice: the Greeks come as the hour arrives: a first sign of the wider gathering
decisions.reason: The Pharisees have just said that "the world has gone after him" (12:19), and now people from beyond Israel come seeking him. Jesus had spoken of other sheep not of this fold (10:16), and John of gathering the scattered children of God (11:52). The scorn of 7:35, that he might go and teach the Greeks, turns out to point the way.

decisions.choice: festival (B, R); to Jerusalem, Passover (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "festival" for the feast. Readable names the place they went up to and the feast, which John has named in 11:55 and 12:1 (meaning decision m2). Balanced puts the Greeks at the end of the sentence, where the Greek puts the weight on them by naming them first.

records.heading: The hour has come

records.greek: οὗτοι οὖν προσῆλθον Φιλίππῳ τῷ ἀπὸ Βηθσαϊδὰ τῆς Γαλιλαίας, καὶ ἠρώτων αὐτὸν λέγοντες· Κύριε, θέλομεν τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἰδεῖν.
records.gloss: These therefore came to Philip the [one] from Bethsaida of the Galilee, and were asking him saying, "Sir, we want the Jesus to see."

L.21: So these came to Philip, the [one] from Bethsaida of Galilee, and were asking him, saying, "Sir, we want to see Jesus."

R.21: They went to Philip, who came from the town of Bethsaida in Galilee. They asked him, "Sir, we would like to meet Jesus."

decisions.choice: Philip from Bethsaida: a disciple with a Greek name from a town on the edge of Gentile country
decisions.reason: Philip came from Bethsaida, the hometown of Andrew and Peter (1:44). The town lay at the north end of the Sea of Galilee, near the Jordan, close to lands where many Gentiles lived, and Philip, like Andrew, bears a Greek name. John does not say why the Greeks went to Philip; that he was approachable to Greek speakers is a likely reason, but it is a guess.

decisions.choice: Sir: a polite address to Philip
decisions.reason: The word is the ordinary courteous way to address a man, as in 4:11 and 20:15. Here it is spoken to Philip, not to Jesus, so nothing more than politeness is meant.

decisions.choice: we want to see Jesus: a request to meet him and speak with him
decisions.reason: The imperfect "were asking" suggests a request pressed politely. "See" here means to meet someone in person, not just to catch sight of him. John uses the same verb of the deeper seeing that comes with believing (1:39; 12:45; 14:9); the request may hint at that, but in the story it is a plain request for a meeting.

decisions.choice: meet (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says "meet" because the Greeks want to talk with Jesus, not only to look at him (meaning decision m3). Literal and Balanced keep "see", the word John wrote.

records.greek: ἔρχεται ὁ Φίλιππος καὶ λέγει τῷ Ἀνδρέᾳ· ἔρχεται Ἀνδρέας καὶ Φίλιππος καὶ λέγουσιν τῷ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: Comes the Philip and tells the Andrew; comes Andrew and Philip and they tell the Jesus.

L.22: Philip comes and tells Andrew; Andrew and Philip come and tell Jesus.

R.22: Philip went and told Andrew. Then the two of them went together and told Jesus.

decisions.choice: Philip and Andrew: two disciples from the same town who bring people to Jesus
decisions.reason: Andrew and Philip appear together in 1:40-44 and 6:5-9, and both bring others to Jesus (1:41-42, 45; 6:8-9). Why Philip first goes to Andrew is not said. He may simply have wanted his fellow townsman with him, or he may have been unsure whether Gentiles should be brought to a Jewish teacher; the text gives no reason.

decisions.choice: the second "comes" is singular though two men are named: a common pattern, with no stress on Andrew
decisions.reason: When a verb stands before two subjects joined by "and", Greek often makes it agree with the first one named. Both men go to Jesus, as the plural "they tell" shows.

decisions.choice: went ... told (B, R); also answered (verse 23)
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("he comes", "he tells") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage (verses 22 and 23).

records.greek: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἀποκρίνεται αὐτοῖς λέγων· Ἐλήλυθεν ἡ ὥρα ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.
records.gloss: The but Jesus answers them saying, "Has come the hour that may be glorified the Son of the Man.

L.23: And Jesus answers them, saying, "The hour has come that the Son of Man may be glorified.

R.23: Jesus answered, "The hour has come. Now the Son of Man will be glorified.

decisions.choice: the hour: the appointed time of Jesus's death and glorification, now arrived
decisions.reason: Until now John has said that Jesus's hour had not yet come (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Here, for the first time, Jesus says that it has. From this point the hour is the time of his passing from this world to the Father (13:1; 17:1). This is the turning point of the Gospel.

decisions.choice: glorified: honored and shown for who he is, through his death, resurrection and return to the Father
decisions.reason: In John, Jesus is glorified when he is lifted up on the cross and raised and returns to the Father (7:39; 12:16; 13:31-32; 17:1, 5). The next verses make plain that the way to glory is death (12:24, 32-33). Glorify is a key term.

decisions.choice: answered them: Andrew and Philip, and perhaps the Greeks with them
decisions.reason: Jesus does not reply to the request directly, and John does not say whether the Greeks met him. His answer speaks to what their coming means: the hour has come, and through his death he will draw all people to himself (12:32). Those addressed are at least Andrew and Philip; soon the crowd is listening too (12:29).

decisions.choice: the Son of Man: the title Jesus uses of himself, from Daniel 7:13-14
decisions.reason: In Daniel 7 one like a son of man receives glory and a kingdom that will not pass away. In John the title is tied to being lifted up and glorified (3:14; 8:28; 13:31), and the crowd will ask about it (12:34).

decisions.choice: hour, at every level
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice keeps "hour" for Jesus's appointed time at Literal and Balanced. Readable may say "time", but in this passage the word comes three times (12:23, 27) and the link with "his hour had not yet come" is the point, so Readable keeps it too. Readable splits the sentence to make the purpose plain.

records.greek: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ἐὰν μὴ ὁ κόκκος τοῦ σίτου πεσὼν εἰς τὴν γῆν ἀποθάνῃ, αὐτὸς μόνος μένει· ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ, πολὺν καρπὸν φέρει.
records.gloss: Truly truly I say to you, if not the grain of the wheat having fallen into the earth should die, it alone remains; if but it should die, much fruit it bears.

L.24: Truly, truly I say to you, unless the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

R.24: I tell you the truth: a grain of wheat must fall into the ground and die. If it does not, it stays just one seed by itself. But if it dies, it grows and produces a great harvest.

decisions.choice: a seed picture: grain sown in the ground seems to die before it grows
decisions.reason: A grain of wheat kept in the storehouse stays as it is. Only when it is buried in the soil and is gone as a seed does it sprout and bear an ear with many grains. Paul uses the same picture for the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:36-37).

decisions.choice: much fruit: the many who will have life through Jesus's death
decisions.reason: The picture applies first to Jesus: by dying he will bring life to many, including the Greeks who have just come (12:20, 32; 11:51-52). Verses 25-26 then apply it to those who follow him. "Bear fruit" returns in 15:2-8.

decisions.choice: remains alone: in its ordinary sense, stays a single grain
decisions.reason: The verb is John's word "remain", here in its everyday sense. The crowd will use it in 12:34: the Christ "remains forever". Jesus's picture answers them in advance: the grain that will not die remains alone.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage.

decisions.choice: stays (B, R); a single grain, one seed by itself; a great harvest (R)
decisions.reason: Following the book-wide choice, the verb is "remain" in its theological sense and the natural word in ordinary senses; Literal keeps "remains" so that the echo in 12:34 shows (meaning decision m3). Readable puts the condition as a plain statement and says what fruit means for a grain of wheat. Balanced keeps "bears much fruit", the phrase of 15:5 and 15:8.

records.greek: ὁ φιλῶν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ ἀπολλύει αὐτήν, καὶ ὁ μισῶν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ τούτῳ εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον φυλάξει αὐτήν.
records.gloss: The [one] loving the life of him loses it, and the [one] hating the life of him in the world this into life eternal will keep it.

L.25: The one who loves their life loses it, and the one who hates their life in this world will keep it into eternal life.

R.25: People who love their own life more than anything will lose it. But people who hate their life in this world, and put it last, will keep it safe and have eternal life.

decisions.choice: love and hate: a way of saying which comes first, not of feeling
decisions.reason: In the Bible "hate" set against "love" often means to love less, to put second (Genesis 29:30-31; Malachi 1:2-3). Luke 14:26 has "hate father and mother" where Matthew 10:37 has "love more than me". Jesus does not ask for disgust at one's own life, but for a life that holds it loosely and puts him first, even to death.

decisions.choice: life: one's own self, the life a person lives
decisions.reason: The word means a person's life, the self who lives it. The same word comes again in 12:27 ("my soul is troubled"), where it is Jesus's inner self.

decisions.choice: the paradox of losing and keeping: clinging to life loses it, giving it up keeps it
decisions.reason: The other Gospels give the saying in similar words (Mark 8:35; Matthew 10:39; Luke 9:24; 17:33). "In this world" marks the life that is let go: life as this world measures it (key term, humanity organized against God). What is kept is kept for eternal life, the life of the age to come. The present "loses" says that such a person is already losing it.

decisions.choice: {{gender:their|his}}
decisions.reason: "The one who" and "whoever" mean any person, man or woman, so the pronoun takes the gender setting. Readable says "people ... their", which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: is losing (B); more than anything, and put it last (R); keep it safe (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced shows the present tense of "loses" (meaning decision m3). Readable keeps "love" and "hate" but explains the idiom (meaning decision m1). "Keep it safe" gives the sense of guarding that the verb has.

records.greek: ἐὰν ἐμοί τις διακονῇ ἐμοὶ ἀκολουθείτω, καὶ ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ ἐκεῖ καὶ ὁ διάκονος ὁ ἐμὸς ἔσται· ἐάν τις ἐμοὶ διακονῇ τιμήσει αὐτὸν ὁ πατήρ.
records.gloss: If me anyone serves, me let him follow, and where am I, there also the servant the my will be; if anyone me serves, will honor him the Father.

L.26: If anyone serves Me, let them follow Me; and where I am, there also My servant will be. If anyone serves Me, the Father will honor them.

R.26: Anyone who serves Me must follow Me. My servant will be with Me wherever I am. And the Father will honor anyone who serves Me.

decisions.choice: serve, servant: one who works for another and attends to his needs
decisions.reason: The verb and the noun are the words for serving, used of waiting at table (2:5, 9; 12:2) and of service in general. They are not the word for a slave, a person owned by another (8:34-35). The stress is on attending to Jesus, which here means going where he goes.

decisions.choice: follow me ... where I am: go the way Jesus goes, through death to the Father, and share his place
decisions.reason: Following Jesus, coming right after the saying about the grain and about losing one's life, means going his way, even to death (13:36-37; 21:18-19). "Where I am" points to where he is going, the Father's presence; he promises that his own will be with him there (14:3; 17:24).

decisions.choice: let him follow: a command, what serving Jesus requires
decisions.reason: The third-person command does not grant permission; it sets the condition. Whoever serves Jesus must follow him.

decisions.choice: the Father will honor him: honor given by God, not by people
decisions.reason: Jesus has said that people seek honor from one another rather than from God (5:41-44). Those who serve him receive honor from the Father himself, as the Son does (8:54).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself, "your" when he speaks to the Father, and "you" when people speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: servant; let them follow (L); Anyone who serves me must follow me (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Servant" is the plain word for this noun at every level; the other word, for one who is owned, is "slave" in Literal (meaning decision m1). Literal gives the pronoun the gender setting, since "anyone" means a man or a woman; Balanced and Readable state the command with "anyone who ... must", which needs no pronoun.

records.greek: Νῦν ἡ ψυχή μου τετάρακται, καὶ τί εἴπω;
records.gloss: Now the soul of me has been troubled, and what may I say?

L.27: Now My soul has been troubled, and what shall I say?

R.27: Now My heart is troubled. What should I say?

decisions.choice: my soul is troubled: Jesus is shaken and distressed in his inner self
decisions.reason: The word for soul is the one translated "life" in 12:25: the self, here as the seat of feeling. The verb for troubled is used of Jesus at Lazarus's tomb (11:33) and at the foretelling of Judas's betrayal (13:21). The perfect tense says he has become troubled and remains so. John does not hide Jesus's anguish at the death ahead of him.

decisions.choice: an echo of the Psalms of distress
decisions.reason: In the Greek of Psalm 6:4-5 the psalmist says that his soul is greatly troubled and asks God to save him; Psalm 42:6-7 and 12 also speak of a downcast, troubled soul. Jesus's words come close to these prayers in both wording and order (troubled soul, then save me). John does not mark a quotation, so the echo is likely but not certain.

decisions.choice: what shall I say: a real deliberative question, Jesus weighing what to pray
decisions.reason: The subjunctive asks what he is to say. In the SBLGNT the question ends here, and the next words are his answer (see the note on the next sentence).

decisions.choice: heart (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says "heart", the everyday word for the inner self where feelings are felt (meaning decision m1). Literal and Balanced keep "soul".

records.greek: πάτερ, σῶσόν με ἐκ τῆς ὥρας ταύτης.
records.gloss: Father, save me out of the hour this.

L.27: Father, save Me from this hour.

R.27: Father, save Me from this hour!

decisions.choice: a real prayer, as the SBLGNT punctuates it: Jesus prays to be saved from the hour, then sets the prayer aside
alternatives: a prayer considered and rejected: "Shall I say, 'Father, save me from this hour'?"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT ends the question at "what shall I say?" and prints "Father, save me from this hour" as a sentence of its own, ending in a full stop. Read so, Jesus truly asks to be spared and at once turns: "But for this reason I came to this hour." The other reading makes it part of the question: "Shall I say, 'Father, save me from this hour'?", a prayer he considers and refuses. The ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, so both readings are possible, and the sense of the passage is the same: Jesus faces the hour and chooses the Father's glory.

decisions.choice: save me from this hour: spare me from the death that is coming
alternatives: bring me safely through this hour
decisions.reason: "This hour" is the hour of 12:23, his death. "Save me out of" most naturally asks to be kept from it, which is why the next words turn against it. Hebrews 5:7 speaks of Jesus praying to the one able to save him out of death, which is sometimes taken to mean bringing him safely through death rather than sparing him from it.

decisions.choice: John's counterpart to the prayer in Gethsemane
decisions.reason: Mark tells how Jesus, his soul very sorrowful, prayed that "the hour might pass from him" and said "Father, ... remove this cup from me; yet not what I will, but what you will" (Mark 14:34-36). John does not tell that scene, but here are the same troubled soul, the same hour, the same prayer to the Father, and the same yielding. Whether John means his readers to recall it is not certain.

decisions.choice: a prayer in its own sentence, with no quotation marks inside Jesus's words
decisions.reason: Following the SBLGNT punctuation (meaning decision m1), every level gives the prayer as words Jesus actually prays, not as a quoted option. Readable ends it with an exclamation mark to show the cry before the turn that follows. The footnote gives the reading as a question.

records.greek: ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦτο ἦλθον εἰς τὴν ὥραν ταύτην.
records.gloss: But on account of this I came into the hour this.

L.27: But on account of this I came to this hour.

R.27: But no. This is the very reason I came: to face this hour.

decisions.choice: for this reason: to go through this hour, for the purpose he names next
decisions.reason: "This" points both back and forward. Jesus came to this hour for the very purpose of the hour itself, his death, and for what it serves: the glory of the Father's name (12:28).

decisions.choice: the cross is the purpose of Jesus's coming, not something that happens to him
decisions.reason: Jesus lays down his life of his own accord (10:17-18) and will not refuse the cup the Father has given him (18:11). He came into the world for this (18:37). The "but" turns from the cry of 12:27 to obedience.

decisions.choice: it was for this very reason (B); But no ... to face this hour (R)
alternatives: But for this purpose I came to this hour
decisions.reason: Balanced puts emphasis on "for this", as the Greek order does. Readable adds "no" to make the turn from the prayer clear, and "to face" to say what coming to the hour means (meaning decisions m1-m2).

records.greek: πάτερ, δόξασόν σου τὸ ὄνομα.
records.gloss: Father, glorify of you the name."

R.28: Father, bring glory to Your name!"

decisions.choice: glorify your name: show who the Father is, in his greatness and love, through what is about to happen
decisions.reason: A name in the Bible stands for the person as he has made himself known (17:6, 26; Psalm 115:1). Jesus's second prayer replaces the first: not escape, but the Father's glory, which will be shown in the Son's death and exaltation (13:31-32; 17:1, 4).

decisions.choice: a prayer like the opening of the Lord's Prayer
decisions.reason: "Father, glorify your name" is close to "Father, may your name be honored" (Matthew 6:9; Luke 11:2). The likeness may be only that both pray for God's name; John does not quote the prayer.

decisions.choice: bring glory to (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says "bring glory to", which keeps the key term and is clearer in everyday speech than "glorify".

records.greek: ἦλθεν οὖν φωνὴ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ· Καὶ ἐδόξασα καὶ πάλιν δοξάσω.
records.gloss: Came therefore a voice out of the heaven, "Both I glorified [it] and again I will glorify [it]."

L.28: So a voice came out of heaven, "I both glorified [it] and will glorify [it] again."

R.28: Then a voice spoke from heaven: "I have brought glory to My name, and I will bring glory to it again."

decisions.choice: a voice from heaven: God the Father speaking
decisions.reason: Heaven stands for God himself. A voice from heaven speaks at Jesus's baptism and transfiguration in the other Gospels (Mark 1:11; 9:7). Here it answers Jesus's prayer at once.

decisions.choice: I have glorified it and will glorify it again: in Jesus's life and signs, and in his death and exaltation
decisions.reason: The Father's name has already been glorified in what Jesus has done, his signs revealing God's glory (2:11; 11:4, 40; 17:4). It will be glorified again in the hour now come, the cross, resurrection and return to the Father (13:31-32; 17:1, 5).

decisions.choice: the unstated object is the Father's name
decisions.reason: Neither verb has an object; both answer "glorify your name" in the line before.

decisions.choice: [it] (L); it (B); my name ... it (R)
decisions.reason: The object is supplied (meaning decision m3): in brackets at Literal, plainly at Balanced, and named at Readable, where the Father speaks of his own name.

records.greek: ὁ οὖν ὄχλος ὁ ἑστὼς καὶ ἀκούσας ἔλεγεν βροντὴν γεγονέναι· ἄλλοι ἔλεγον· Ἄγγελος αὐτῷ λελάληκεν.
records.gloss: The therefore crowd the [one] having stood and having heard was saying thunder to have happened; others were saying, "An angel to him has spoken."

L.29: So the crowd that was standing [there] and had heard was saying that it had thundered; others were saying, "An angel has spoken to Him."

R.29: The crowd standing there heard the sound. Some of them said it was thunder. Others said, "An angel has spoken to Him."

decisions.choice: the crowd heard a sound but did not grasp what was said
decisions.reason: The crowd heard something, but some took it for thunder, and others knew it was speech without receiving it as God's own word. John does not say whether any of them made out the words. In the same way the companions of Paul heard a sound but did not understand the voice (Acts 9:7; 22:9).

decisions.choice: thunder and angels: ways people of the time thought God might speak
decisions.reason: In Scripture thunder goes with God's voice (Exodus 19:16-19; 2 Samuel 22:14; Psalm 29:3; Job 37:4-5), and angels bring God's word to people (Genesis 22:11; Luke 1:13). Both groups sense that something from heaven has happened, yet neither hears the Father answering his Son.

decisions.choice: the sound; Some of them
decisions.reason: Readable says the crowd heard a sound, and adds "some of them" to set beside "others": the Greek says the crowd said one thing and others another (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν· Οὐ δι’ ἐμὲ ἡ φωνὴ αὕτη γέγονεν ἀλλὰ δι’ ὑμᾶς.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said, "Not because of me the voice this has come but because of you.

L.30: Jesus answered and said, "Not because of Me has this voice come, but because of you.

R.30: Jesus answered, "This voice did not speak for My sake. It spoke to help you.

decisions.choice: for your sake: so that the crowd might believe that the Father sent Jesus
decisions.reason: Jesus did not need the voice to know that the Father hears him. At Lazarus's tomb he gave thanks aloud for the same reason, "because of the crowd standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me" (11:42).

decisions.choice: not ... but: a sharp contrast that puts the whole purpose on the hearers
decisions.reason: The voice was not given for Jesus's sake at all, but for theirs. Even so, most of them did not understand it (12:29), and few believed (12:37).

decisions.choice: This voice came for your sake, not for mine (B); did not speak for my sake. It spoke to help you (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the positive part first, the natural order for this kind of contrast; Literal keeps the Greek order. Readable says what "for your sake" means in two short sentences.

records.greek: νῦν κρίσις ἐστὶν τοῦ κόσμου τούτου, νῦν ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ κόσμου τούτου ἐκβληθήσεται ἔξω·
records.gloss: Now judgment is of the world this, now the ruler of the world this will be cast out;

L.31: Now is [the] judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out.

R.31: Now is the time for this world to be judged. Now Satan, the ruler of this world, will be thrown out.

decisions.choice: now is the judgment: the world is judged at the cross, in the hour that has come
decisions.reason: "Now" is the hour of 12:23. By the way it treats Jesus, the world shows what it is and is judged (3:18-19), and the ruler of this world is condemned (16:11). The same events are the world's judgment and the defeat of its ruler.

decisions.choice: world: humanity organized against God
decisions.reason: Both times here "this world" is not the created order but human life as it stands apart from God and under a ruler opposed to him (15:18-19; 17:14). World is a key term.

decisions.choice: the ruler of this world: Satan
decisions.reason: Jesus calls him so again in 14:30 and 16:11. He is the devil, who puts it into Judas's heart to betray Jesus (13:2, 27). Paul uses a similar title (2 Corinthians 4:4; Ephesians 2:2). Being cast out means losing his hold over the world.

decisions.choice: will be cast out (SBLGNT)
alternatives: will be cast down (a few witnesses)
decisions.reason: A few witnesses, among them some early versions, read "will be cast down" instead of "cast out". Nearly all manuscripts read "out", and the sense is close. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the time of judgment (B); the time for this world to be judged; Satan (R); driven out (B); thrown out (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "the time" to show that "now" means this moment, the hour. Readable names Satan, whom the title means (meaning decision m3); the speaker is Jesus, who knows who the ruler is. "Driven out" and "thrown out" say what being cast out means today.

records.greek: κἀγὼ ἐὰν ὑψωθῶ ἐκ τῆς γῆς, πάντας ἑλκύσω πρὸς ἐμαυτόν.
records.gloss: And I if I am lifted up out of the earth, all I will draw to myself."

L.32: And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all [people] to Myself."

R.32: And when I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to Myself."

decisions.choice: lifted up: raised on the cross, and by that exalted
decisions.reason: As in 3:14 and 8:28, the verb means both to raise something high and to exalt someone. The next verse says that it points to the kind of death Jesus would die, and "from the earth" fits being raised on a cross; but in the Greek of Isaiah 52:13 the LORD's servant "will be lifted up and glorified", and here the lifting up draws all people to him. Every level keeps "lifted up" with both senses.

decisions.choice: if I am lifted up: a sure event, not a doubtful one
decisions.reason: "If" here means "when", as in 14:3 ("if I go and prepare a place for you"). Jesus has no doubt it will happen. "And I" is emphatic: set against the ruler of this world cast out (12:31), Jesus will be lifted up and draw people to himself.

decisions.choice: all: all people, Gentiles as well as Jews
decisions.reason: The word is masculine and refers to people. Coming just after the Greeks' request (12:20-23), it means that people of every nation, not only Israel, will be drawn to Jesus (10:16; 11:52). John does not say here that every person will believe; the next verses tell of many who did not (12:37).

decisions.choice: all people (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: A few important manuscripts, among them P66 and the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, with some early Latin copies, read the neuter "all things". The great majority read "all people", which fits the context of the Greeks' coming. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: draw: bring people to himself by his own power
decisions.reason: The same verb is used in 6:44, where no one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws him. Now Jesus, lifted up, does the drawing. The verb is also used of hauling in a net full of fish (21:6, 11).

decisions.choice: lifted up, with no "on the cross"; As for me, when (B); all [people] (L); all people (B, R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice keeps "lifted up" at every level with no addition, as at 3:14 and 8:28; the narrator explains it in the next verse (meaning decision m1). Balanced shows the emphatic "I" with "As for me" and says "when" (meaning decision m2). "All people" already includes men and women and needs no gender setting.

records.greek: τοῦτο δὲ ἔλεγεν σημαίνων ποίῳ θανάτῳ ἤμελλεν ἀποθνῄσκειν.
records.gloss: This now he was saying signifying by what kind of death he was about to die.

L.33: Now this He was saying, signifying by what kind of death He was about to die.

R.33: He said this to show how He was going to die: lifted up on a cross.

decisions.choice: the narrator explains Jesus's words
decisions.reason: John steps out of the scene to tell the reader what "lifted up" means. He uses the same phrase again in 18:32, when Pilate's handing Jesus over leads to crucifixion, and of Peter's death in 21:19.

decisions.choice: what kind of death: crucifixion, death by being raised up on a cross
decisions.reason: The Jewish authorities could not lawfully put a man to death (18:31-32), and the Roman form of execution was crucifixion, in which the condemned was raised on a cross. "Lifted up from the earth" pointed to this. "Signifying" means indicating by a hint rather than saying outright.

decisions.choice: lifted up on a cross (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of death was meant (meaning decision m2). The narrator, not Jesus, gives this explanation, so the addition puts no knowledge into a character's mouth.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη οὖν αὐτῷ ὁ ὄχλος· Ἡμεῖς ἠκούσαμεν ἐκ τοῦ νόμου ὅτι ὁ χριστὸς μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, καὶ πῶς λέγεις σὺ ὅτι δεῖ ὑψωθῆναι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου;
records.gloss: Answered therefore him the crowd, "We heard out of the law that the Christ remains into the age, and how say you that it is necessary to be lifted up the Son of the Man?

L.34: So the crowd answered Him, "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever, and how do You say that it is necessary for the Son of Man to be lifted up?

R.34: The crowd answered Him, "The Law tells us that the Christ will remain forever. So why do You say the Son of Man has to be lifted up?

decisions.choice: the Law: the Scriptures as a whole
decisions.reason: "The Law" here is not only the books of Moses but the Scriptures generally, as in 10:34 and 15:25, where Psalms are quoted as the Law.

decisions.choice: the Christ remains forever: the promise of an everlasting king from David's line
decisions.reason: No single verse says these words. In the Greek of Psalm 89:37-38 David's offspring "will remain forever"; Isaiah 9:7 promises a kingdom with no end, Ezekiel 37:25 that David will be prince forever, and Daniel 7:14 that the dominion of the one like a son of man will not pass away. Which passage the crowd had in mind is uncertain.

decisions.choice: the crowd takes "lifted up" to mean being taken away by death
decisions.reason: They understand enough to see that Jesus speaks of leaving the earth, and that does not fit a Messiah who remains forever. They put together his words about the Son of Man (12:23) and about being lifted up (12:32). Their "remains" echoes Jesus's grain that "remains alone" unless it dies (12:24).

decisions.choice: the Christ: the title, God's anointed King
decisions.reason: With the article it is a title, the Messiah the people were waiting for (1:20, 41; 7:41-42).

decisions.choice: So how can you tell us (B); So why do you say ... has to (R); must (B); The Law tells us (R)
alternatives: How is it that you say (Literal)
decisions.reason: The question "how do you say" is a protest, not a request for information; Balanced and Readable put it as English protests, as at 8:33. "Must" (Balanced) and "has to" (Readable) for "it is necessary", as at 3:14. Readable says "tells us" for "we have heard from".

records.greek: τίς ἐστιν οὗτος ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου;
records.gloss: Who is this the Son of the Man?"

L.34: Who is this Son of Man?"

decisions.choice: a puzzled question: what kind of Son of Man is this, who must be lifted up?
decisions.reason: The crowd is not asking for a definition of the title. They cannot fit a Son of Man who must die with the Messiah they expect, so they ask what figure Jesus can mean. Their question may also carry doubt about Jesus himself.

decisions.choice: Jesus does not answer directly
